quickAnswer: In 2026, the Basilica Cistern (Yerebatan Sarnıcı) runs two daily sessions: Daytime (09:00–18:30, 1,950–2,250 TL for foreign visitors) and Night Shift (19:30–22:00, 3,000 TL), separated by a one-hour changeover. Operated by Istanbul's municipal Kültür AŞ rather than the Ministry of Culture, it is excluded from MuseumPass Istanbul and takes 30 to 45 minutes to explore.

body.text: How do daytime tickets differ from evening Night Shift admission?

Daytime admission (09:00–18:30) costs 1,950 to 2,250 TL for foreign visitors in 2026 and covers standard self-guided access along the elevated walkways, while [Night Shift admission](https://yerebatan.com/night-shift-en/) (19:30–22:00) costs 3,000 TL for quieter galleries, specialized lighting, and occasional evening concerts or multimedia programming. The cistern closes between 18:30 and 19:30 to clear daytime crowds.

Official online tickets are sold through [Passo](https://www.passo.com.tr/en/event-group/yerebatan-sarnici-the-basilica-cistern-istanbul-muze-biletleri/247613), the municipal ticketing partner, which lets you bypass the sidewalk cash queue on Yerebatan Caddesi. Because [2026 ticket prices](https://istanbul-tourist-information.com/basilica-cistern-updated-info/) have adjusted during the year and Night Shift sessions occasionally pause for private corporate rentals, verify active evening availability before building your dinner plan around a 19:30 entry. For most first-time visitors, an early 09:00 daytime slot offers the best balance of cost and breathing room; Night Shift pays off mainly if you want low-crowd photography or a confirmed acoustic performance.

body.text: Where are the Medusa heads and weeping column inside?

Both landmarks sit along the one-way elevated steel walkway installed during the 2022 restoration. You pass the carved Weeping Column (Hen's Eye Column) roughly two-thirds of the way into the hall, and reach the two colossal Medusa head column bases at the far northwest corner just before the path turns back toward the exit stairs.

Built under Byzantine Emperor Justinian I between 527 and 565, the 140-by-70-meter underground reservoir rests on 336 recycled Roman marble columns ([Kültür.İstanbul](https://kultur.istanbul/yerebatan-sarnici-muzesi/)). The Weeping Column stands out for its damp surface and teardrop-shaped peacock-eye carvings—traditionally linked to enslaved laborers who died during construction. At the far northwest corner, two monumental Roman Medusa blocks serve as plinths—one turned sideways and one upside down—most likely positioned to match the exact height required by the shafts above them rather than for mythic superstition.
Why is Basilica Cistern NOT included in MuseumPass?

The Basilica Cistern is excluded from [MuseumPass İstanbul](https://muze.gov.tr/urun-detay?CatalogNo=WEB-MSP01-05-009) because it is operated by Kültür AŞ, a cultural company owned by the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality (İBB), rather than the national Ministry of Culture and Tourism. Municipal museums use a completely separate ticketing system and revenue stream from national Ministry sites.

This administrative split surprises travelers who assume one pass covers all of Sultanahmet. Just steps away, Hagia Sophia, Topkapı Palace (Milli Saraylar), and the Basilica Cistern (İBB Kültür AŞ) are each run by three different institutions with three separate tickets. Always budget the cistern as a standalone line item and purchase only from the on-site booth or [Passo](https://www.passo.com.tr/en/event-group/yerebatan-sarnici-the-basilica-cistern-istanbul-muze-biletleri/247613)—skip street resellers offering marked-up "skip-the-line" bundles outside the gate.
How long does the visit take?

A comfortable walk through the entire Basilica Cistern takes 30 to 45 minutes, even when pausing for photos at the Weeping Column, the Medusa heads, and the contemporary sculpture installations set among the columns. Add 15 to 30 minutes if you plan to queue at the street box office between 11:00 and 15:00.

Because the cavern remains cool year-round with humidity approaching 96% and occasional water dripping from the vaulted brick ceiling, wear non-slip shoes and keep camera lenses dry. Flash photography is prohibited to preserve the lighting design. The cistern exits onto Alemdar Caddesi, a two-minute walk from the Sultanahmet T1 tram stop and Hagia Sophia.

faq.q: How much are Basilica Cistern tickets in 2026?
faq.a: Foreign-visitor daytime entry is 1,950–2,250 TL (verify current door pricing on Passo), while the evening Night Shift ticket is 3,000 TL; audio guides cost roughly 300 TL extra.

faq.q: Is the Basilica Cistern open on Mondays and Tuesdays?
faq.a: Yes. The cistern opens seven days a week from 09:00 to 18:30 for daytime visits and 19:30 to 22:00 for Night Shift, making it easy to slot into Monday or Tuesday itineraries.

faq.q: Can you use MuseumPass Istanbul at the Basilica Cistern?
faq.a: No. Because it is managed by Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality's Kültür AŞ rather than the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, MuseumPass is never accepted.

faq.q: Where is the entrance to the Basilica Cistern?
faq.a: The entrance is on Yerebatan Caddesi No: 1/3 in Sultanahmet, directly across the street from Hagia Sophia and two minutes from the Sultanahmet T1 tram stop.

faq.q: Are strollers or wheelchairs able to enter the cistern?
faq.a: Access down into the cistern involves a steep 52-step staircase, so strollers must be folded and carried; contact [info@yerebatan.com](mailto:info@yerebatan.com) in advance for current accessibility arrangements.

faq.q: Is the Night Shift worth the extra cost?
faq.a: It is worthwhile if you want uncrowded reflection photos or a scheduled evening concert. If you simply want to see the columns and Medusa heads, a 09:00 daytime entry saves up to 1,050 TL per person.
